title: Chapter 16 – The Tree That Charges Back
html:
Grandfather comes down to the quarry gap in his sleeping robe, with the old sword in his hand and a lamp-bearer behind him, and looks at the glowing prints for a long time without saying a word.

The sun is fully up now. Without the Moonlamp, the prints have gone invisible, so Lin Jian lights it again and holds it low, and the old man bends over the gravel and follows the little blue boots with his eyes, step by step, up the terrace and along the library wall. Father is there too, white and unshaven, with a thin square of yellow paper in his hand. It is a Mirror Memory, one of the rarest slips in his case, a talisman that holds a single moment of light the way a bowl holds water. Father presses it to the latch, murmurs the word, and the paper darkens. When he lifts it, the whole scene is printed on it in miniature: the blue prints, the blue palm, the stone door.

"It will keep a month," he says. His voice is hoarse. "Then the ink fades."

"A month is enough," says Grandfather.

"For what?" That is Old Hu, who has come up the slope behind them with his rod over his shoulder and the look of a man who has not slept either. "Begging your pardon, Patriarch. But it's a footprint and a smudge. Your steward will say he went down at night to check the pit. A man in his position has every right to inspect the defenses of the house. He'll say he turned the pins for his own reasons. The arbiter will ask why a steward works with his hands in the dark. He'll say he's a careful man."

"Yes," says Grandfather.

"So?"

"So the paper goes in Wenyuan's strongbox. And we change nothing."

Hu stares at him.

"We do not change the lock," says the old man. "We do not warn the pit's guards. We do not so much as look at my second son across the breakfast table. He has put his hand on the pin, and on the door, and he will do it again. Every time he does, the dust will light the way, and the paper will fill, and when the box is full we will take it into daylight." He looks down at the sword in his hand, as if surprised to find it there. "A man who thinks he is unobserved is the most careful liar in the world, Hu. And the most careless thief."

Lin Jian, behind the lamp, says nothing. He is looking at his grandfather's hand on the hilt. It is perfectly steady. Only the knuckles are white.

"There is one thing more," Grandfather says. He turns, and for the first time looks directly at his grandson. "Lin Jian."

"Yes, Grandfather."

"You found this because you check the pit each morning, and you check it each morning because Old Hu taught you to. Is that right?"

It is not. They all know it is not. Hu opens his mouth, and Lin Jian says, quite evenly, "Yes, Grandfather."

The old man looks at him a moment longer. Then he nods, slowly, the way he nods at a ledger that balances for reasons he has chosen not to examine.

"Then you will go on checking," he says, "and you will tell me, and no one else."

\ \ \*

That afternoon, Lin Jian sits in his father's workshop and drinks tea.

It is a peculiar thing, tea in a talisman maker's room. A Heat Plate talisman is pinned to the underside of the table, a small orange circuit the size of his palm that keeps the iron kettle at a gentle simmer without a fire. A Dust-Away slip is stuck to the shelf of ink bottles, quietly pulling the powder out of the air. A Clear Light slip glows over the desk, fed by a crystal chip. Father has made a small paradise out of these cheap, ordinary charms, and Lin Jian has sat in it for the better part of two years.

Father is drawing. He has been drawing since dawn. His hand shakes less when he works, and neither of them mentions it.

"Father."

"Mm?"

"I need three Royal Spirit Chains."

The brush stops.

It is a thing he has said carefully, in the voice of a boy asking for sweets. Royal Spirit Chain is not a household talisman. It is an advanced binding charm, a Yellow-grade slip requiring a steady hand, a clean line, and a drop of the draftsman's own blood in the ink. Father makes perhaps a dozen a year, for the Sect's Talisman Pavilion, at a price that would feed the household for a month.

Father lays the brush down. He turns on his stool and looks at his youngest son for a long moment.

"What for?"

"To hold something still."

"What something?"

Lin Jian says nothing.

"I see." Father rubs his forehead with the heel of his hand. "You are sixteen years old, Jian. You are not going into the forest."

"No, Father."

"You are not going into the forest, and you are not going to tell me you are not going into the forest."

"I'm not going to tell you," Lin Jian says, "that I'm not going into the forest."

For a moment Father's face does something complicated. Then, to Lin Jian's astonishment, he laughs. It is a short, painful, tired sound, the first real laugh the house has heard in three weeks, and it breaks in the middle and turns into something else, and he covers his eyes with one shaking hand.

"Your mother said you'd do this," he says. "She said, he won't ask, and when he asks, it will be for something exactly right. I told her she was wrong." He drops the hand. "Sit."

Lin Jian sits.

Father reaches into the case at his elbow and takes out a flat wooden box. It holds three slips of heavy cream paper, each marked with a tight, complex circuit of interlocking rings, the lines drawn in a dark, rusty ink. He sets them in a row on the desk.

"Royal Spirit Chain," he says. "The line is a knot, Jian. Look at it. It is a single stroke, no breaks. If you try to draw it as separate pieces it fails, because a chain cannot be assembled. It has to be one thing. And the ink has my blood in it, which means it answers to a hand that knows how it was made." He lays two fingers on the first slip. "When you throw it, don't say the word. Think the knot. Think of a closed loop, tightening. It will catch whatever you aim it at and hold it for as long as your Qi lasts. Six breaths with you. Eight, with me. Ten if I were whole."

"Thank you."

"I am not finished." Father looks at him. "You will take all three. You will use no more than one at a time, and you will use it on a thing you are certain you can finish before it breaks. A chain is not a plan. It is a short breath held to let you think."

"Yes, Father."

"And when you come home," his father's voice cracks, very slightly, "you will walk through that door, and you will let me see you. Every time. Do you understand? Whatever else, you will let me see you."

"Yes, Father."

"Good." The older man picks up the brush. "Now drink your tea. It's getting cold."

Lin Jian drinks his tea. It is excellent. He has never in his life tasted anything so bitter.

\ \ \*

He finds the thing he is looking for by accident.

Fourth Uncle's patrol reports come in at dusk, delivered in a battered tin tube by whoever drew the short straw, and read aloud in the guardhouse over rice and salt pork. Lin Jian is not supposed to be there. He is on the roof, lying flat on the tiles with his ear to a loose slate, as he has been most evenings for a month, and it is only because he is listening for something else, any mention of feathers, any report of bloodless animals, that he hears the corporal say, with the flat gloom of a man reading out a death:

"West stream path. Walking Elm's moved again."

"How far?"

"Eighty paces down the bank since last month. It's on the near side of the dry bed now."

"Mother of heaven. It'll be at the terraces by summer."

"It won't leave its hill," says a third voice, older. "They don't. It'll pull itself up to the edge of the roots and glare. But I'd stay off the west path after the new moon. Just in case."

"What's it eaten?"

"A deer, maybe two. Whatever blunders into thirty paces. Nobody's seen it charge in a year."

Lin Jian lies very still on the tiles.

He knows the name. Everyone does. The Walking Elm is one of the sights of the western ridge, a tree-beast of the first rank, peak tier, that has stood on the edge of the dry stream for longer than anyone's grandfather can remember, as broad as a granary and as tall as the gatehouse, black-barked, red-leaved, silent. Old women tell children that it is a sleeping god. The children are warned never to look it in the eye.

A first-rank beast at the peak, Mao told the cousins once. The equivalent, in the Qi Refining ladder, of a cultivator at the seventh or eighth layer. Strong enough to break a man's back with a single blow of a root. Slow enough, if you are careful, to avoid.

Nobody's seen it charge in a year.

He turns it over slowly in his head, lying there in the cold, listening to the guards' voices fade.

The beast is a fighter. Not a clever one, but a real one, a thing with weight, speed, and a body that does not die when pricked. A practice ground made by nature. A place to learn what the pins and the talismans and the spells will do against something that wants to kill him, without the extra complication of a man who thinks.

He can't practice on Mao. Mao is a cousin, and has a conscience. He can't practice on Feng, who is convalescing and furious. He can't practice on Hu, who would stop him.

But a tree that has not moved in a year will not complain.

I need to know, he thinks. Before the Blood Shadow comes back. I need to know what I can actually do.

\ \ \*

He goes at the new moon.

Not alone, exactly. He tells Hu the night before, in the forge, in a voice so flat that it takes the old man a moment to understand what he is being told.

"The west stream," says Hu. "The dry bed."

"Yes."

"The Elm."

"Yes."

"Absolutely not."

Lin Jian says nothing. He picks up a piece of scrap iron and turns it over, and does not look up.

For a long time the forge is silent but for the pop of the coals. Then Hu lets out a breath so long and tired that it seems to deflate him.

"The Elm," he says, "has three weak points. The sap-gland at the base of the trunk, where the main roots join. The crown, which you can't reach. And the eyes, which are the knots. You see them. Three knots on the trunk, at a man's height, in a triangle. They look like the face of a sleeping god. They are not. They are where the nerve of the thing runs closest to the surface." He picks up his mug and drains it. "A blow to the eyes will make it charge. A blow to the sap-gland will make it die. And in between, there is you, being a smear on a root."

"I know."

"I'm telling you what I know. I'm not telling you to go."

"I understand."

"Good." The old man's one eye is cold as a blade. "Because if I were telling you to go, I would tell you to go at dawn, when the dew is on the leaves and the sap is low. I would tell you to wear your boots, because the ground there is shale. I would tell you to count its charge, which takes four breaths from rest to full speed, and which goes straight, never in a curve, because the thing cannot turn at speed any more than a boulder can." He sets down the mug. "And I would tell you not to be there when the sun comes over the ridge, because after that it wakes properly. I am telling you none of this. Go to bed."

\ \ \*

He is there an hour before dawn.

The west stream path is a gray ribbon in the dark, winding along the lip of the dry bed between slabs of broken shale. The air is cold and smells of stone and old leaves. He has a pack on his back with the three Royal Spirit Chains, a coil of rope, two packets of salt, and a bundle of talismans: four Flame-Bursts, a Mirror Guard in the pocket of his short robe, and a stub of chalk. Under his short robe, against his ribs, lies the Nine-Pin Belt, warm as a living thing.

He goes the last hundred paces on his belly.

The Walking Elm stands at the edge of the dry bed like a ruined tower. In the faint gray light it is enormous: a trunk wider than a cart, black and ridged as a cliff, rising to a crown that spreads over the whole of the bank. The leaves are the deep red of old wine. Nothing moves in them. A few of its roots, thick as a man's body, have heaved up out of the shale and lie coiled on the surface like the arms of a sleeping squid.

And in the trunk, at a man's height, three round knots. Two above, one below.

They look exactly like a face.

Lin Jian stays flat behind a slab of shale. He is a hundred and ten paces from the trunk, and his spiritual sense, now at forty paces, does not reach. So he does what he always does when the world is out of range. He finds something that has come to him.

A single red leaf has blown downslope and lies on the shale an arm's length away. He reaches out and lays two fingers on it.

```
[Scan: Elm Leaf]
Source: Walking Elm (first-rank beast, peak)
Tissue: wood-attribute Qi, dense; sap pressure high
Notable: salt intolerance — cell walls rupture above 4% brine
Nerve cluster: three nodes, trunk-face (primary), sap-gland (root base, primary)
Estimated mass: 11,000 lb. Charge velocity: ~9 m/s
CE: +3
```

He reads it twice. Then he sits very still and thinks about salt intolerance.

Every tree he has ever seen dies if you pour brine on its roots. It is the oldest trick in any gardener's book, older than pepper, older than the Cleansing slip. A first-rank beast does not die, of course. But it does not like it. It is a thing of wood and sap and cell walls, and cell walls are stubborn about being asked to hold what they do not want.

The sap-gland at the base of the trunk, he thinks. If I could get it wet.

Salt dissolves in water. He has two packets of salt and a stream bed that has been dry since the autumn. He has no water.

He has a pocket full of fire.

\ \ \*

The beast wakes at the first light of the sun.

Lin Jian has been waiting for it. He has circled the bank in a wide arc, moving from slab to slab, and settled at last on a ledge of shale twenty paces upslope from the trunk, with the stream bed on his right and the thorn scrub at his back. He has driven six of the Belt's pins into the ledge in the hexagon pattern, dust-gray in the dust-gray earth, and tied the rope across their tops to look like a fallen branch. He has chalked a line at his feet. He has placed the first of the packets, the salt, upwind, on a flat rock beside the trunk, rolled in a Flame-Burst slip.

The sun clears the ridge, and light floods the red leaves, and the Elm opens its eyes.

It is not a sound. It is a pressure. The leaves rustle all at once, in a ripple that runs up the whole height of the crown, and then fall still, and the three knots in the trunk, the two above, the one below, shift, with a slow, grinding creak like a door in a cellar. And they are no longer knots. They are three round amber pupils, burning, fixed on the ledge.

Lin Jian does not breathe.

Four breaths, he thinks. From rest to full speed. Counting begins when the first root leaves the ground.

The Elm does not move. It looks at him.

Then the thickest of its roots, the one nearest, uncoils from the shale, slowly, like a snake in sunlight, and slams down. The ledge shakes. A shower of splinters rains on his head.

He throws the Flame-Burst.

It is the one he has put on the salt packet. It goes off with a flat soft crack, and the packet bursts open in a cloud of white grit, and the grit drifts, glittering in the sunlight, across the Elm's trunk.

The beast screams.

It is not a scream a mouth could make. It is the sound of a great hull flexing under pressure, a vast groan from the trunk that rattles the loose stones under his feet. The leaves on the nearest branches go gray and curl. The bark where the salt has landed blisters and weeps pale sap.

And the beast charges.

One. The roots come up out of the ground, a dozen at once, thick as barrels, and the trunk tilts. Two. The whole tree lurches forward on its roots like a man stepping off a cliff, and the shale cracks. Three. It is faster than he thought, eleven thousand pounds of wood bearing down at a run, the ground shaking, and Lin Jian can see the knots, the three amber eyes, getting larger.

Four.

He steps to the left, a single swift Cloudstep, and the Elm goes past him like an avalanche.

It does not turn. It cannot. It goes straight, down the line of the ledge, over the chalk mark, through the hexagon.

The six pins light.

The ground between them stops being ground. The Elm's front roots punch down into it as through wet clay, and the whole trunk lurches, and the beast roars again, and tries to pull itself free.

Sixty breaths, Lin Jian thinks. Maybe seventy, with a thing this big.

He is already running.

He covers the twenty paces to the trunk in six strides, the Belt's glow bright against his ribs, the pins singing. The Elm sees him. A great root whips round, low and fast. He drops, slides under it, feels it pass over his back like a gale, rolls to his feet beneath the trunk, and slams his palm flat against the bark at the base.

```
[Scan: Sap-Gland]
Location: root base, 0.4 m below grade
Sap pressure: 380 kPa
Salt tolerance: 3.8%
Weak point: gland wall, thin at three seam points (marked)
```

Three seam points. They appear in his mind's eye as three small glowing rings in the bark, in a rough triangle, no larger than coins.

He pulls the first Royal Spirit Chain from his sleeve, thinks the knot, and snaps it onto the largest root.

Silver light wraps the root in a spiral. The root stiffens. The Elm shrieks, and the grip of the pit tightens, and the whole beast shudders.

Eight breaths. He has eight, at best.

He steps back three paces. He lifts his right hand, fingers together like a blade. Qi runs down his arm, water-cold, shaped by the pattern his mother taught him. The Tidal Spear is a clumsy thing at the fifth layer, a bolt of water the size of a spear. He does not want a spear. He wants a needle.

He thins it. He compresses it. He pushes it through a channel so narrow his hand trembles, until what leaves his fingers is not a bolt but a hair of pressurized water, a bright, silent line no thicker than a thread.

It goes through the first seam point like a needle through silk.

The Elm screams. Pale sap spurts out of the hole, dribbles, and then catches the light. He turns his hand. The second line, the second seam. A third.

Sap fountains from the base of the trunk. And where the sap runs, the salt grit on the bark drifts down into the wounds, and the gray blistered patches spread like a rash, and the leaves on every branch, all at once, rattle and drop.

The chain breaks. The root swings free and slams down beside him, a hand's breadth away. Shale explodes. A splinter the length of his forearm plows through his short robe and into the meat of his left shoulder, and he cries out and falls backward, tearing at the wound.

The Elm pulls one front root out of the pit. The ground sucks at it, but it comes, and it plants it on the shale and heaves.

Twenty breaths left on the pit. Maybe fewer.

He drags himself up on one knee. His left arm is wet to the elbow. The beast looms over him, three amber eyes, forty feet of red leaf against the sky, and he looks up into it and thinks, quite clearly: I have one more thing.

He tears the second Royal Spirit Chain out of his sleeve, thinks the knot, and does not throw it at the root.

He throws it at the eyes.

Silver light wraps the face of the Elm in a mask. The beast jerks its great head upward, away from the binding, and its whole trunk lifts, and for the first time since it woke it exposes the pale, wet, seeping base of the trunk and the three small marked rings.

Lin Jian raises his right hand.

He feeds it everything he has.

The needle that leaves his fingers is the thinnest, brightest, coldest line he has ever shaped. It does not pierce the first ring. It does not pierce the second. It passes through all three at once, through the seam between them, and out the far side of the trunk.

For one breath nothing happens.

Then the sap-gland bursts.

\ \ \*

When he can hear again, there is a great quiet in the stream bed.

The Walking Elm lies on its side along the length of the ledge, black bark gray with salt, leaves scattered like a red snowfall. Its roots are curled. The three amber eyes have gone dull. A thin pale fluid seeps from the base of the trunk into the shale and soaks away.

Lin Jian sits in the dust with his back against a rock and holds his shoulder.

The splinter is still in him. He can feel it grate when he breathes. It is a ragged shard of ironwood a finger wide and long as a spoon, and it has gone in under the collarbone at an angle that makes him feel sick. He grips it with his good hand. He pulls.

It comes out in a rush of blood and a wave of white.

He lies there for a while with his eyes shut, pressing the heel of his hand to the hole, breathing through his teeth. The Belt has gone quiet at his ribs. The pins are fine, he can feel it; the pit is done, and the chains have burned out. He opens one eye and looks at the sky. It is very blue. A single crow is circling, high up.

Crows, he thinks. Again.

He takes a long breath, and the first thing that comes to him is not pain, or triumph, or fear.

It is arithmetic.

Salt, three seconds. Chain, eight breaths. Needle, three hits, one miss. The pit held for sixty. The charge was nine meters a second, not eight. He had been wrong about how fast it could turn. He had been wrong about the shoulder.

Three mistakes, he thinks. And I'm alive.

He pulls his short robe off and bandages the wound with a strip torn from his tunic and one of the Cleansing slips from his pocket, held flat under the wrap until the sting dies. It is not good. It will do until he gets home.

Then he crawls over to the fallen beast, and lays his hand on its bark.

```
[Scan: Walking Elm (deceased)]
Core: wood-attribute spirit pith (first-rank, peak) — intact
Usable material: heartwood (spirit-timber, Yellow grade), sap-gland (preserved), 3 amber knots
Creation Energy: +11
CE: 41 / 400
```

Eleven. He had thought it would be more. But the beast is not the point. The beast is a measure, and the measure says that Lin Jian, at the fifth layer of Qi Refining, with ten years of cultivation behind him and a pocket full of paper, can kill an eleven-thousand-pound first-rank monster in a morning.

If I plan. If I'm lucky. If the ground is right.

If the thing doesn't think.

The man in the feather cloak will think.

He pries the three amber knots free with the point of a pin. They are warm in his palm, glossy as river stones. He wraps them in cloth and puts them in the pack. The pith comes out in a single hard greenish lump the size of an egg. The heartwood he leaves; it is far too big. Then he stands, and sways, and looks once more at the fallen tree.

At the foot of the trunk, half-hidden among the roots, something catches the light.

He kneels and brushes the shale away.

A dead fox lies curled beneath the roots, small, russet, perfectly still. It has been there a day, perhaps two. There is no wound on it. The fur is clean. The eyes are closed.

But when he lays his fingers on its flank, there is nothing inside it at all. It is as light as straw.

```
[Scan: Fox (deceased)]
Cause of death: exsanguination via transdermal draw
Foreign Qi: blood-attribute, trace
Similarity to residue at Salt Hollow: 64%
Estimated time since death: 41 hours
```

Sixty-four percent.

Not the same man. Not the man with the burned eye. A cousin, a brother, a pupil. The same art, and the same hunger.

Lin Jian kneels in the dry stream bed beside the dead tree, in the morning light, with blood drying on his shoulder, and understands that something has been here before him, and watched, and counted, and gone away again to report.

On the bark of the Elm, three paces from his hand, someone has pressed a palm. The print is shallow and dark, reddish-brown, dried and cracked like old paint. He steps close and lays two fingers beside it.

```
[Scan: Palm Mark]
Pigment: iron ochre + blood-attribute Qi (trace)
Pattern: three-dot survey sign, Blood Shadow Sect (scout's waymark)
Meaning (inferred): "ground surveyed; no guard; return"
Age: ~41 hours
```

Ground surveyed. No guard. Return.

He stands up very slowly, and looks at the ridge, and the path, and the empty sky. There is nothing there. There is only the wind in the dead leaves, and a single crow turning, high and patient, in the blue.

He is not the only one who has been practicing on the west path. Someone else has been counting the distance from the dry bed to the terraces, and the wall, and the gate.
